transcription.tex: Question 4

Bernhard has to pass an examination to get into law school. He can take the examination as many times as he likes and his probability of passing on any one attempt is 0.3.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that:\par (i) he passes on his third attempt\par (ii) he takes at least four attempts to pass.\par \textbf{b} State two assumptions that you have used in your model.

Let $X$ count the attempts up to and including the first pass. The failure probability is $1-0.3=0.7$.\par \textbf{a} (i) Two failures followed by a pass give $\mathrm P(X=3)=0.7^2(0.3)=0.147$.\par (ii) At least four attempts means failing the first three. $\mathrm P(X\ge4)=0.7^3=0.343$.\par \textbf{b} Attempts are independent and the probability of passing is the same on every attempt.
Question 10

Frances, Georgina and Holly agree who is to do the washing up by playing a game. They each roll a fair six-sided dice and record whether the outcome is odd or even. If two of them get the same outcome and the third one gets a different outcome, that person has to wash up. If no decision is reached they play again.\par Given that each game is independent, find the probability that:\par \textbf{a} a decision is reached on the third game\par \textbf{b} it takes at least four games to reach a decision.

Let $X$ count the games up to and including the first decision.\par \textbf{a} Each of three players rolls odd or even, so there are $2^3=8$ equally likely outcomes. Only OOO and EEE fail to reach a decision. Thus $p=(8-2)/8=3/4$.\par Two undecided games followed by a decision give $\mathrm P(X=3)=(1/4)^2(3/4)=3/64=0.0469$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} At least four games means the first three are undecided. $\mathrm P(X\ge4)=(1/4)^3=1/64=0.0156$ (4 d.p.).
Question 11

Julian works in a village pharmacy and he finds that the long-term average number of customers per hour is 4. Find the probability that:\par \textbf{a} at least 5 customers come in during a randomly chosen hour.\par He records the number of customers during each hour on a particular day.\par Find the probability that:\par \textbf{b} the first occurrence of 5 or more customers is in the 5th hour\par \textbf{c} he goes through a whole 8-hour shift with no single hour having 5 or more customers.

\textbf{a} Model the number of customers in an hour by $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(4)$. From the tables, $p=\mathrm P(X\ge5)=1-\mathrm P(X\le4)=1-0.6288=0.3712$.\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count hours up to and including the first with five or more customers. Assuming independent hours at the same rate, $Y\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)$.\par Four preceding hours must have fewer than five customers. $\mathrm P(Y=5)=(0.6288)^4(0.3712)=0.0580$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} For all eight hours to have fewer than five customers, $\mathrm P(Y>8)=(0.6288)^8=0.0244$ (4 d.p.).

transcription.tex: Question 7

Vincent records $X$, the number of attempts it takes him to parallel-park his car in a particular space.\par \textbf{a} State a suitable probability distribution for $X$.\par \textbf{b} State two assumptions that must be made for this distribution to be appropriate.\par Given that $\mathrm P(X=2)=0.16$ and that $p<0.5$, find:\par \textbf{c} $p$, the probability that Vincent parks correctly on each single attempt\par \textbf{d} the expected number of attempts Vincent takes\par \textbf{e} the variance of $X$.

\textbf{a} Use a geometric distribution, $X\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)$, counting attempts up to and including the first success.\par \textbf{b} Each attempt is independent and the probability of parking successfully in that space is constant.\par \textbf{c} $\mathrm P(X=2)=(1-p)p=0.16$, so $p^2-p+0.16=0$.\par $p=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{(-1)^2-4(0.16)}}{2}=\dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{0.36}}2=\dfrac{1\pm0.6}2$.\par The two roots are $0.2$ and $0.8$. Since $p<0.5$, choose $p=0.2$.\par \textbf{d} $\mathrm E(X)=1/p=1/0.2=5$ attempts.\par \textbf{e} $\operatorname{Var}(X)=(1-p)/p^2=0.8/0.04=20$.
Question 8

Uma has a bag of marbles, 15% of which are blue. She puts her hand in the bag and pulls out a marble at random. If the marble is not blue, she puts it back in the bag and tries again.\par \textbf{a} Calculate:\par (i) the mean\par (ii) the variance of the number of marbles she pulls out, up to and including the first blue one.\par Calculate the probability that:\par \textbf{b} she pulls out 4 marbles\par \textbf{c} she pulls out at least 8 marbles\par \textbf{d} she pulls out fewer marbles than expected.

Let $X$ be the number of draws up to and including the first blue marble. Replacement makes $p=0.15$ on each draw.\par \textbf{a} (i) $\mathrm E(X)=1/0.15=20/3=6.67$ (2 d.p.).\par (ii) $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\dfrac{1-0.15}{0.15^2}=\dfrac{17\times400}{20\times9}=\dfrac{340}{9}=37.78$ (2 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Three non-blue marbles followed by a blue give $\mathrm P(X=4)=0.15(0.85)^3=0.0921$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} At least eight draws means no blue in the first seven. $\mathrm P(X\ge8)=0.85^7=0.3206$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} $X$ is an integer. $\mathrm P(X<20/3)=\mathrm P(X\le6)=1-0.85^6=0.6229$ (4 d.p.).
Question 9

Tabitha the cat is trying to catch fish out of a garden pond. The probability that she catches a fish at each attempt is 0.12.\par \textbf{a} State two assumptions that must be made to model this situation as a geometric distribution.\par \textbf{b} Find:\par (i) the probability that Tabitha takes two attempts to catch a fish\par (ii) the probability that Tabitha takes at least three attempts to catch a fish.\par \textbf{c} Find the expected number of attempts Tabitha takes to catch a fish and the variance.\par Once Tabitha has caught one fish, she tries to catch a second one.\par \textbf{d} Find the probability that she needs three attempts to catch her first fish, and three further attempts to catch her second fish.\par \textbf{e} Find the probability that she caught the first fish on the second attempt, and the second fish on the fifth attempt.

\textbf{a} Assume a constant probability of catching a fish on each attempt and independence between attempts.\par \textbf{b} Let $X$ count attempts up to and including the first catch. The failure probability is $0.88$.\par (i) $\mathrm P(X=2)=0.12(0.88)=0.1056$.\par (ii) $\mathrm P(X\ge3)=0.88^2=0.7744$.\par \textbf{c} $\mathrm E(X)=1/0.12=100/12=25/3=8.33$ (2 d.p.).\par $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\dfrac{1-0.12}{0.12^2}=\dfrac{0.88\times10\,000}{144}=\dfrac{8800}{144}=\dfrac{550}{9}=61.11$ (2 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Treat the waiting times for successive fish as independent. Three attempts for each means $\mathrm P(X=3)^2=[0.12(0.88)^2]^2\approx0.09293^2=0.0086$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{e} Catching the first fish on attempt 2 and the second on attempt 5 means two attempts followed by three further attempts.\par $\mathrm P(X=2)\mathrm P(X=3)=[0.12(0.88)][0.12(0.88)^2]\approx0.1056(0.09293)=0.0098$ (4 d.p.).
Question 10

Simeon, a tailor, records the number of faults, $X$, per metre of cloth.\par He finds that there are, on average, 0.8 faults per metre.\par \textbf{a} State, giving any assumptions you make, a suitable probability distribution for $X$.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that in a randomly chosen metre of cloth there are more than two faults.\par Simeon cuts the cloth into one-metre lengths.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that the first time he encounters a metre of cloth with more than two faults is in the 7th metre.\par \textbf{d} Find the expectation and variance of the number of metres of cloth he cuts before he finds a metre length with more than two faults.\par If a metre of cloth containing two or more faults occurs before Simeon has cut 3 one-metre lengths, he sends that roll of cloth back to the manufacturers.\par \textbf{e} Find the probability that he sends back two consecutive rolls of cloth.

\textbf{a} Assume faults occur independently, singly and at a constant average rate per metre. Then $X\sim\operatorname{Po}(0.8)$.\par \textbf{b} $p=\mathrm P(X>2)=1-\mathrm P(X\le2)\approx1-0.9526=0.0474$.\par \textbf{c} Let $Y$ count metres up to and including the first with more than two faults. $Y\sim\operatorname{Geo}(p)$. Six preceding metres have at most two faults.\par $\mathrm P(Y=7)=(1-p)^6p\approx(0.9526)^6(0.0474)=0.0354$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Including the metre on which he finds the faults, $\mathrm E(Y)=1/0.0474\approx21$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=(1-0.0474)/0.0474^2\approx424$, to the nearest whole number. Counting only the preceding metres gives $Y-1$, with mean about 20 and the same variance.\par \textbf{e} The return rule uses two or more faults. Its one-metre probability is $q=\mathrm P(X\ge2)=1-\mathrm P(X\le1)=1-0.8088=0.1912$.\par Let $Z\sim\operatorname{Geo}(q)$ count metres until the first such length. A roll is returned if $Z\le2$. Thus $\mathrm P(Z\le2)=1-(1-0.1912)^2=0.3458$.\par For independent rolls the probability of returning both is $0.3458^2=0.1196$ (4 d.p.).

One way in which we can use a biased coin, with probability of heads of \(p\), to model a fair coin, is to use the following process:\par Flip the unfair coin twice.\par If the first flip is Heads and the second Tails, declare “Heads”.\par If the first flip is Tails and the second Heads, declare “Tails”.\par Otherwise, go back to step 1 until a declaration is made.\par Determine the average number of flips required of the biased coin, before we can declare “Heads” or “Tails”.

For independent flips, HT and TH each have probability \(p(1-p)\). A pair gives a declaration with probability \(q=2p(1-p)\).\par Let \(X\) count pairs up to and including the first declaration. Then \(X\sim\mathrm{Geom}(q)\) and \(E(X)=1/[2p(1-p)]\).\par Each pair uses two flips, so the expected number of flips is \(2E(X)=\boxed{1/[p(1-p)]}\), for \(0<p<1\).

transcription.tex: Question 6

Francesca is playing a series of games with her sister. The probability that Francesca wins any particular game is 0.55.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that Francesca wins her fourth game on the sixth attempt.\par \textbf{b} State two assumptions that have to be made for the model used in part a to be valid.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that Francesca wins her third game on the fifth attempt, given that she won the first game.\par \textbf{d} Find the probability that Francesca wins at least seven out of the first ten games.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count the games up to the fourth win. $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(4,0.55)$. Three of the first five games must be wins, and game six must be a win.\par $\mathrm P(X=6)=\binom53(0.55)^4(0.45)^2=0.1853$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Games are independent and the probability of winning is the same for every game.\par \textbf{c} Given the first win, she needs two more wins in four further games, the second on the fourth. Let $Y\sim\operatorname{NB}(2,0.55)$ count those games.\par $\mathrm P(Y=4)=\binom31(0.55)^2(0.45)^2=0.1838$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Let $A$ count wins in the first ten games. $A\sim\operatorname{B}(10,0.55)$. Then $\mathrm P(A\ge7)=1-\mathrm P(A\le6)\approx1-0.7340=0.2660$.
Question 7

Gerald is trialling a new drug that in previous trials has cured patients 80% of the time.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that Gerald’s drug cures the seventh patient on the tenth trial.\par \textbf{b} State two assumptions that have to be made for the model used in part a to be valid.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that Gerald has cured at least seven patients in the first twelve trials.\par \textbf{d} Find the probability that it takes more than 20 trials to cure 15 patients.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count trials up to the seventh cure. $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(7,0.8)$. Six cures occur in the first nine trials and the tenth patient is cured.\par $\mathrm P(X=10)=\binom96(0.8)^7(0.2)^3=0.1409$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Assume independent trials and the same cure probability for each patient.\par \textbf{c} Let $Y$ count cures in twelve trials, so $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(12,0.8)$.\par $\mathrm P(Y\ge7)=1-\mathrm P(Y\le6)\approx1-0.0194=0.9806$.\par \textbf{d} Let $Z$ count cures in twenty trials, so $Z\sim\operatorname{B}(20,0.8)$. Needing more than twenty trials for the fifteenth cure means there are at most fourteen cures so far.\par $\mathrm P(Z\le14)=0.1958$ (4 d.p.).
Question 8

Harriet is conducting scientific experiments. Each experiment is independent and the probability of any single experiment working is 0.1.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that Harriet achieves her second successful experiment on her 20th attempt.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that it takes her more than 30 experiments to get four successes.\par \textbf{c} Find the probability that Harriet achieves her fourth successful experiment on her 30th attempt given that she was first successful on the fifth attempt.\par \textbf{d} Find the probability that Harriet is successful in at least three experiments out of the first 25.

\textbf{a} Let $X$ count attempts up to her second success. $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(2,0.1)$. Choose the position of the first success among the first 19 attempts.\par $\mathrm P(X=20)=\binom{19}{1}(0.1)^2(0.9)^{18}=0.0285$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{b} Let $Y$ count successes in 30 attempts. $Y\sim\operatorname{B}(30,0.1)$. If she still needs a fourth success, $Y\le3$, with probability $0.6474$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} After her first success on attempt 5, there are $30-5=25$ further attempts. Let $Z\sim\operatorname{NB}(3,0.1)$ count attempts until three further successes.\par $\mathrm P(Z=25)=\binom{24}{2}(0.1)^3(0.9)^{22}=0.0272$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} Let $A$ count successes in 25 attempts. $A\sim\operatorname{B}(25,0.1)$.\par $\mathrm P(A\ge3)=1-\mathrm P(A\le2)\approx1-0.5371=0.4629$.
Question 10

A darts player is trying to hit the bullseye. She throws darts at the board until she scores three bullseyes. The random variable $D$ is the number of darts she needs to throw.\par \textbf{a} State a suitable distribution to model $D$.\par \textbf{b} Given that the probability of her hitting the bullseye on each attempt is 0.35, find the probability that:\par (i) it takes her seven throws to score the three bullseyes\par (ii) it takes her at least eight throws to score the three bullseyes\par (iii) it takes her nine throws, given that she hits the bullseye on her first throw.\par \textbf{c} Give one reason why this model may not accurately represent the situation.

\textbf{a} Let $p$ be the probability of hitting the bullseye. $D\sim\operatorname{NB}(3,p)$ counts throws up to the third hit.\par \textbf{b} (i) Use $p=0.35$ and $1-p=0.65$. Two of the first six throws must hit, and the seventh must hit.\par $\mathrm P(D=7)=\binom62(0.35)^3(0.65)^4=0.1148$ (4 d.p.).\par (ii) Let $E$ count hits in seven throws, so $E\sim\operatorname{B}(7,0.35)$. Then $\mathrm P(D\ge8)=\mathrm P(E\le2)=0.5323$.\par (iii) Given a hit on throw one, two more hits are needed in the remaining eight throws, with the second on the eighth of these. Let $F\sim\operatorname{NB}(2,0.35)$ count the further throws.\par $\mathrm P(F=8)=\binom71(0.35)^2(0.65)^6=0.0647$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Practice may improve the player's accuracy, changing her probability of a hit.

transcription.tex: Question 6

The random variable $X$ has negative binomial distribution with mean 6 and variance 3.\par Find:\par \textbf{a} the value of $p$ and the value of $r$\par \textbf{b} $\mathrm P(X=4)$.\par \textbf{Problem-solving} Write two equations involving $r$ and $p$ and solve them simultaneously.

\textbf{a} $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(r,p)$. The mean gives $\mathrm E(X)=r/p=6$, hence $r=6p$.\par The variance gives $r(1-p)/p^2=3$, hence $r(1-p)=3p^2$.\par Substitute $r=6p$: $6p(1-p)=3p^2$. Since $p\ne0$, divide by $p$ to obtain $6(1-p)=3p$.\par Thus $6=9p$, so $p=6/9=2/3$ and $r=6p=4$.\par \textbf{b} Four successes in four trials means every trial succeeds. $\mathrm P(X=4)=(2/3)^4=16/81=0.1975$ (4 d.p.).
Question 7

Kelly and her classmates are taking part in a competition where students take turns attempting to solve a puzzle. The probability that each student solves the puzzle is 0.7. The random variable $X$ represents the number of students who need to attempt to solve the puzzle before five have solved it.\par \textbf{a} State two conditions that are necessary for $X$ to be modelled by a negative binomial distribution.\par \textbf{b} Using a negative binomial model, find the mean and standard deviation of $X$.

\textbf{a} Students' attempts must be independent and each student must have the same probability of success.\par \textbf{b} $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(5,0.7)$. The mean is $\mathrm E(X)=5/0.7=50/7=7.143$ (3 d.p.).\par $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\dfrac{5(1-0.7)}{0.7^2}=\dfrac{1.5}{0.49}\approx3.0612$.\par $\sigma=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}=1.750$ (3 d.p.).
Question 8

In each trial of an experiment, four fair coins are spun.\par \textbf{a} Find the probability that all four coins show the same result.\par \textbf{b} Find the probability that all four coins show the same result for the third time on the sixth trial.\par \textbf{c} Find the expected number of trials needed in order for the coins to show the same result 12 times.

\textbf{a} Whichever face appears on the first coin, the other three must match it. Their probability of doing this is $(1/2)^3=1/8=0.125$.\par Alternatively, the four independent spins have $2^4=16$ equally likely outcomes. Only HHHH and TTTT qualify, giving $2/16=1/8$.\par \textbf{b} Let $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(3,0.125)$ count trials up to the third match. Two of the first five trials must qualify, followed by a match on trial six.\par $\mathrm P(X=6)=\binom52(0.125)^3(0.875)^3=0.0131$ (4 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} Let $Y\sim\operatorname{NB}(12,0.125)$ count trials until the twelfth match. Then $\mathrm E(Y)=12/0.125=96$ trials.
Question 9

Michelle is playing darts. The probability that she hits ‘treble twenty’ with any one dart is $p$.\par Given that the expected number of throws needed in order for her to hit the ‘treble twenty’ 3 times is 18.75, find:\par \textbf{a} the value of $p$\par \textbf{b} the variance.\par Michelle gets some coaching. Given that her new probability of hitting the ‘treble twenty’ is 0.24, find:\par \textbf{c} the expected number of throws needed to hit the ‘treble twenty’ 5 times\par \textbf{d} the probability that it takes her more than the expected number of throws to hit the ‘treble twenty’ 5 times.

\textbf{a} Let $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(3,p)$ count throws up to the third treble twenty. $\mathrm E(X)=3/p=18.75$, so $p=3/18.75=1/6.25=4/25=0.16$.\par \textbf{b} $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\dfrac{3(1-4/25)}{(4/25)^2}=\dfrac{3\times21\times25\times25}{25\times16}=\dfrac{1575}{16}=98.44$ (2 d.p.).\par \textbf{c} After coaching, let $Y\sim\operatorname{NB}(5,0.24)$ count throws to the fifth treble twenty.\par $\mathrm E(Y)=5/0.24=500/24=125/6=20.83$ (2 d.p.).\par \textbf{d} More than the expected number of throws means 21 or more. Let $Z$ count treble twenties in the first 20 throws, so $Z\sim\operatorname{B}(20,0.24)$. The fifth treble twenty has yet to occur if $Z\le4$.\par $\mathrm P(Y>20)=\mathrm P(Z\le4)=0.4561$ (4 d.p.).
Question 10

Norman picks marbles at random from a bag that contains 100 marbles. He notes the colour and replaces the marble. He repeats the process until he has selected a green marble $r$ times. The random variable $X$ represents the total number of times he selects a marble.\par \textbf{a} State a distribution that could be used to model $X$.\par \textbf{b} Given that the mean and standard deviation of $X$ are 12 and 6 respectively, calculate:\par (i) the number of green marbles in the bag\par (ii) the value of $r$.\par Alison selects marbles from the same bag. She notes the colour but does not replace the marble each time.\par \textbf{c} Give a reason why a negative binomial distribution is not a suitable model for this situation.\par \textbf{d} Find the probability that Alison picks her second green marble on her third pick.

\textbf{a} $X\sim\operatorname{NB}(r,p)$, where $p$ is the probability of selecting a green marble. Replacement keeps the success probability constant.\par \textbf{b} (i) $\mathrm E(X)=r/p=12$, so $r=12p$. The variance is $6^2=36$, giving $r(1-p)/p^2=36$ or $r(1-p)=36p^2$.\par Substitute $r=12p$. Then $12p(1-p)=36p^2$. Since $p\ne0$, divide by $12p$. Thus $1-p=3p$, so $p=1/4=0.25$.\par There are $100p=100(0.25)=25$ green marbles.\par (ii) $r=12p=3$.\par \textbf{c} Without replacement the probability of selecting a green marble depends on the earlier draws. The constant-probability assumption fails.\par \textbf{d} Write $G$ for green and $N$ for not green. The sequences giving the second green on the third pick are $G,N,G$ and $N,G,G$.\par $\mathrm P(G,N,G)+\mathrm P(N,G,G)=\dfrac{25}{100}\dfrac{75}{99}\dfrac{24}{98}+\dfrac{75}{100}\dfrac{25}{99}\dfrac{24}{98}=\dfrac{50}{539}=0.0928$ (4 d.p.).
